description: A perennial aquatic herb rooted in mud with large, round, waxy, water-repellent leaves held above the water on long prickly stalks, and showy pink or white flowers with many petals. The flower develops a flat-topped seed pod and the plant has a creeping, segmented rhizome.
cultural_significance: The lotus is India's national flower and a symbol of purity and spiritual growth, associated with Lakshmi, Brahma and Vishnu. Padma and Pushkara are mentioned in the Rigveda and Atharvaveda and are common in Vedic and Puranic imagery.
habitat: Still, shallow, fresh water such as ponds, lakes and slow rivers in warm climates.

uses.title: Burning sensation, fever and thirst
uses.detail: Flowers and petals are described as cooling (Sheeta) and used in Pitta-related heat, thirst and burning sensations.

uses.title: Diarrhoea and dysentery
uses.detail: Rhizome and seed preparations are traditionally used for loose motions; described as Grahi.

uses.title: Skin and cosmetic care
uses.detail: Petals and rhizome paste are traditionally applied to soothe heat rashes and brighten the skin (Varnya).

uses.title: Calming and sleep
uses.detail: Seeds (makhana-like lotus seeds) and flower tea are traditionally considered calming for the mind.

uses.title: Antioxidant research
uses.detail: Studies on alkaloids such as nuciferine show antioxidant and metabolic effects in laboratory work; clinical evidence is limited.

ayurveda.vedic_note: Lotus (Pushkara, Padma) appears in Vedic literature, including the Rigveda and Atharvaveda, and is an enduring symbol in Vedic ritual and later tradition. I am not citing individual hymn numbers.

preparations.name: Padma kwatha or hima
preparations.method: Steep or boil petals or stamen in water and strain.

preparations.name: Kamala kesara churna
preparations.note: Used in cooling and bleeding-related formulations.

preparations.name: Lotus seed (makhana-like) preparation
preparations.method: Dry roast or cook seeds in milk or in cooking.

preparations.name: Lotus root (kamal kakdi) dish
preparations.note: A food use of the rhizome; avoid raw due to parasite risk.

precautions: Raw lotus root from natural water bodies can carry parasites, so cook it well. Lotus seed alkaloids (neferine, liensinine) may lower blood pressure and may add to the effects of sedatives and blood pressure medicines. Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy. Do not harvest from polluted water; plants take up toxins.

cultivation.propagation: Rhizome segments or seeds (nick the hard coat before soaking)
cultivation.harvest: Flowers in summer; rhizomes in autumn; seeds when pods dry

conservation_status: Not threatened; widely cultivated and naturalised.
fun_fact: Lotus leaves have a micro-textured surface that repels water, an effect called the lotus effect, which inspires self-cleaning materials.

regions.name: South Asia (Widely cultivated)
regions.note: Ponds and lakes across the subcontinent

regions.name: Kashmir Valley
regions.note: Famous lotus gardens on Dal Lake
